sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a non-parametric framework for Bayesian inference, allowing for both predictions and uncertainty estimates. The flexibility of GPs comes from their kernel functions, which encode prior assumptions about function structure.

However, the expressiveness of a standard GP is limited by its kernel (Pravesh and Roi 2020). Choosing an appropriate kernel often requires domain expertise and trial and error, and a fixed kernel may fail to capture the complex, multi-scale structure present in real data. This motivated Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) (Damianou and Lawrence 2013), which compose multiple GP layers into a hierarchy that can learn rich representations automatically.

DGPs stack multiple GP layers so that each layer’s output becomes the next layer’s input. This composition allows the model to learn features at multiple levels of abstraction — much like deep neural networks — while retaining the principled uncertainty quantification of the GP framework. The price of this flexibility is tractability: although each layer is individually Gaussian, the composition produces a non-Gaussian joint distribution over latent functions, making exact inference intractable.

This dissertation provides an exploration of Gaussian Processes and Deep Gaussian Processes, progressing from foundational theory to advanced architectures. We derive standard GP regression from first principles, show how composing GPs into deep hierarchies yields greater expressiveness at the cost of tractability, and develop the variational inference machinery needed to train these models at scale.

Finally, we apply DGPs to real-world datasets within finance, demonstrating their ability to capture complex patterns and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates that are crucial for risk based decision making. We compare DGPs to standard GPs and standard machine learning models, and show that GP based models lead to better calibrated uncertainty estimates.
We begin by deriving the theory of standard GPs.

sec.title: 2. Towards Gaussian Processes
sec.p: The problem in supervised machine learning is inferring functional relationships between input variables and observed outputs from a set of training examples. Given dataset \mathbf{D} = \{(\boldsymbol{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n𝐃={(𝐱i,yi)}i=1n where \boldsymbol{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^D𝐱i∈ℝD is an input vector and y_i \in \mathbb{R}yi∈ℝ is the corresponding output, we aim to learn some function f: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}f:ℝD→ℝ that represents the underlying mapping y = f(\boldsymbol{x}) + \epsilony=f(𝐱)+ϵ, where \epsilonϵ is a noise term.

In a classical frequentist approach, we typically define the function ff as a parametric model and estimate it by means of a finite set of parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟. For example, in linear regression we have f(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{\phi}^\top \boldsymbol{x}f(𝐱)=𝛟⊤𝐱, and we aim to find the best estimate \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}𝛟̂ such that \boldsymbol{y_i} \approx \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}^\top \boldsymbol{x}_i𝐲𝐢≈𝛟̂⊤𝐱i for all ii. Within Bayesian statistics, we place a prior distribution on the parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟, and then compute a posterior distribution p(\boldsymbol{\phi} | \mathbf{D})p(𝛟|𝐃) that captures updated beliefs about the parameters after observing the data (Bishop 2006; Murphy 2013).

In these so-called parametric models, the function ff is fully specified by a finite set of parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟. This number and structure of parameters is fixed in advance, and therefore the function space of ff is limited by the choice of model. Further to this, the choice of parameters is often required before observing the data, and therefore requires domain expertise to select an appropriate model for the data.

In contrast to frequentist approaches that specify a parametric model and estimate its parameters via maximum likelihood (Bishop 2006), Gaussian processes place a prior directly on an infinite-dimensional function space (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; D. J. MacKay 1998; Williams and Rasmussen 1995). Observed data then reduces uncertainty, yielding a posterior distribution that captures updated beliefs about the function.
This section outlines the theory of GPs for regression tasks, starting from the weight-space view of Bayesian linear regression and building up to the function-space view of GPs.

sec.title: 2.1 The Weight Space View
sec.p: Before moving to the full function space perspective, it is helpful to build intuition through a finite-dimensional parametric approach. The weight space view treats regression as Bayesian inference over a weight vector. We show how the the structure of the resulting predictive distribution can be expressed in terms of inner products between inputs, which naturally motivates the transition to Gaussian processes (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; D. J. MacKay 1998).

We begin with a linear model of the form
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{w}, \qquad(1)f(𝐱)=𝐱⊤𝐰,(1)

where \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^D𝐰∈ℝD is a weight vector. To make this more general, consider an expansion of basis functions (Bishop 2006)
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} w_j \phi_j(\mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^\top \mathbf{w}, \qquad(2)f(𝐱)=∑j=1Mwjϕj(𝐱)=𝛟(𝐱)⊤𝐰,(2)

where \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = [\phi_1(\mathbf{x}), \ldots, \phi_M(\mathbf{x})]^\top𝛟(𝐱)=[ϕ1(𝐱),…,ϕM(𝐱)]⊤ is a vector of basis functions mapping the input to an MM-dimensional feature space, with weights \mathbf{w} = [w_1, \ldots, w_M]^\top𝐰=[w1,…,wM]⊤. This is more general than the simple linear model, allowing non-linear relationships through the choice of basis functions \phi_j(\cdot)ϕj(⋅), without breaking linearity in the parameters \mathbf{w}𝐰.

Given training data \mathcal{D}𝒟, our goal is to learn the weights \mathbf{w}𝐰. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) would yield a single point estimate \hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{MLE}} = (\Phi^\top\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^\top\mathbf{y}𝐰̂MLE=(Φ⊤Φ)−1Φ⊤𝐲 (Bishop 2006; Murphy 2013). However, this ignores how different weight vectors may explain the observed data equally well, but make very different predictions in unobserved region.

sec.title: 2.2.1 Prior and Likelihood
sec.p:
A Bayesian approach addresses this by placing a prior distribution over \mathbf{w}𝐰, turning the problem into Bayesian linear regression (Bishop 2006; Gelman et al. 2025). A natural choice is a zero-mean Gaussian prior:
p(\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \Sigma_p), \qquad(3)p(𝐰)=𝒩(𝐰∣𝟎,Σp),(3)

where \Sigma_p \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times M}Σp∈ℝM×M is the prior covariance matrix. A common prior is \Sigma_p = \sigma_w^2 \mathbf{I}Σp=σw2𝐈, which gives i.i.d. Gaussian weights with variance \sigma_w^2σw2 (D. J. C. MacKay 1992).

Modelling each observation as y_i = f(\mathbf{x}_i) + \epsilon_iyi=f(𝐱i)+ϵi with independent noise \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_n^2)ϵi∼𝒩(0,σn2), we get a likelihood for a single observation of the form
p(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(y_i \mid \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top \mathbf{w}, \sigma_n^2). \qquad(4)p(yi∣𝐱i,𝐰)=𝒩(yi∣𝛟(𝐱i)⊤𝐰,σn2).(4)

Assuming independence across observations, and conditioning on \mathbf{w}𝐰, we have that the joint likelihood over \mathcal{D}𝒟 is
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathcal{N}(y_i \mid \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top \mathbf{w}, \sigma_n^2). \qquad(5)p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝐰)=∏i=1n𝒩(yi∣𝛟(𝐱i)⊤𝐰,σn2).(5)

Collecting observations into the design matrix \Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times M}Φ∈ℝn×M with \Phi_{ij} = \phi_j(\mathbf{x}_i)Φij=ϕj(𝐱i) (Rasmussen and Williams 2008) (see Appendix 6.2 for the explicit construction), Equation 5 becomes a single multivariate Gaussian:
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y} \mid \Phi \mathbf{w}, \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}). \qquad(6)p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝐰)=𝒩(𝐲∣Φ𝐰,σn2𝐈).(6)

sec.title: 2.2.2 Posterior over Weights
sec.p:
Applying Bayes’ theorem gives the posterior distribution over weights:
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w})}{p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X})}. \qquad(7)p(𝐰∣𝐗,𝐲)=p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝐰)p(𝐰)p(𝐲∣𝐗).(7)

Because the Gaussian prior is a product of Gaussians, and the likelihood is also Gaussian, the posterior is Gaussian as well (Bishop 2006; Bernardo and Smith 2000). The prior and likelihood are conjugate distributions, so the posterior is in the same family as the prior, this is called conjugacy (Gelman et al. 2025) and is a key property that allows for closed-form inference. Evaluating the posterior gives the covariance

and posterior mean
\bar{\mathbf{w}} = \sigma_n^{-2} \Sigma_w \Phi^\top \mathbf{y}. \qquad(9)𝐰‾=σn−2ΣwΦ⊤𝐲.(9)

The posterior distribution over the weights is therefore
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \bar{\mathbf{w}}, \Sigma_w). \qquad(10)p(𝐰∣𝐗,𝐲)=𝒩(𝐰∣𝐰‾,Σw).(10)

sec.title: 2.3 Predictive Distribution
sec.p:
This posterior distribution captures uncertainty about the weights given the observed data. We can use it to make predictions at a new input \mathbf{x}_*𝐱* by marginalising over the weight posterior:
p(f_* \mid \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) = \int p(f_* \mid \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) \, d\mathbf{w}, \qquad(11)p(f*∣𝐱*,𝐗,𝐲)=∫p(f*∣𝐱*,𝐰)p(𝐰∣𝐗,𝐲)d𝐰,(11)

where f_* = f(\mathbf{x}_*)f*=f(𝐱*). Since f(\mathbf{x}_*) = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^\top \mathbf{w}f(𝐱*)=𝛟(𝐱*)⊤𝐰 is a linear function of \mathbf{w}𝐰, the marginal p(f_* \mid \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y})p(f*∣𝐱*,𝐗,𝐲) is also Gaussian (Bishop 2006, chap. 3). sec.title: 2.4 From Weight Space to Function Space
sec.p:
The predictive distribution in Equation 12 is expressed in terms of the feature map \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟. However, we can note that \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟 only appears through inner products of the form \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^\top \Sigma_p \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}')𝛟(𝐱)⊤Σp𝛟(𝐱′). This motivates defining a kernel function (interchangeably called a covariance function) as an inner product in the feature space: (Schölkopf 2002; Rasmussen and Williams 2008)
k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^\top \Sigma_p \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}'), \qquad(13)k(𝐱,𝐱′)=𝛟(𝐱)⊤Σp𝛟(𝐱′),(13)
which measures similarity between inputs in the feature space, weighted by the prior covariance \Sigma_pΣp.

With this definition, collecting pairwise kernel evaluations over the training set into the kernel matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}K∈ℝn×n with K_{ij} = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)Kij=k(𝐱i,𝐱j), and the vector of cross-covariances \mathbf{k}_* \in \mathbb{R}^n𝐤*∈ℝn with [\mathbf{k}_*]_i = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_*)[𝐤*]i=k(𝐱i,𝐱*), we can rewrite the predictive equation entirely in terms of the kernel. This can be done by reparametrizing the posterior covariance \Sigma_w = (\sigma_n^{-2}\Phi^\top\Phi + \Sigma_p^{-1})^{-1}Σw=(σn−2Φ⊤Φ+Σp−1)−1 using the matrix inversion lemma (Rasmussen and Williams 2008, Equation A.9),
(A + UCV)^{-1} = A^{-1} - A^{-1}U\bigl(C^{-1} + VA^{-1}U\bigr)^{-1}VA^{-1}, \qquad(14)(A+UCV)−1=A−1−A−1U(C−1+VA−1U)−1VA−1,(14)

setting A = \Sigma_p^{-1}A=Σp−1, U = \Phi^\topU=Φ⊤, C = \sigma_n^{-2}\mathbf{I}C=σn−2𝐈, V = \PhiV=Φ, which gives the equivalent n \times nn×n expression:
\Sigma_w = \Sigma_p - \Sigma_p\Phi^\top\bigl(\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I} + \Phi\Sigma_p\Phi^\top\bigr)^{-1}\Phi\Sigma_p. \qquad(15)Σw=Σp−ΣpΦ⊤(σn2𝐈+ΦΣpΦ⊤)−1ΦΣp.(15)

In matrix form K = \Phi\Sigma_p\Phi^\topK=ΦΣpΦ⊤ and \mathbf{k}_* = \Phi\Sigma_p\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)𝐤*=ΦΣp𝛟(𝐱*). Substituting Equation 15 into the predictive mean \mathbb{E}[f_*] = \sigma_n^{-2}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^\top\Sigma_w\Phi^\top\mathbf{y}𝔼[f*]=σn−2𝛟(𝐱*)⊤ΣwΦ⊤𝐲:
\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[f_*] &= \sigma_n^{-2}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^\top\Sigma_p\Phi^\top\mathbf{y} - \sigma_n^{-2}\mathbf{k}_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}K\mathbf{y} \\ &= \mathbf{k}_*^\top\bigl[\sigma_n^{-2}\mathbf{I} - \sigma_n^{-2}(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}K\bigr]\mathbf{y} \\ &= \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y}, \end{aligned} 𝔼[f*]=σn−2𝛟(𝐱*)⊤ΣpΦ⊤𝐲−σn−2𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1K𝐲=𝐤*⊤[σn−2𝐈−σn−2(K+σn2𝐈)−1K]𝐲=𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐲,

where the last step uses \sigma_n^{-2}(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}[(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})-K] = (K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}σn−2(K+σn2𝐈)−1[(K+σn2𝐈)−K]=(K+σn2𝐈)−1. Substituting into the variance \operatorname{Var}[f_*] = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^\top\Sigma_w\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*) + \sigma_n^2Var[f*]=𝛟(𝐱*)⊤Σw𝛟(𝐱*)+σn2:
\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}[f_*] &= \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^\top\Sigma_p\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*) - \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_* + \sigma_n^2 \\ &= k(\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{x}_*) - \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_* + \sigma_n^2. \end{aligned} Var[f*]=𝛟(𝐱*)⊤Σp𝛟(𝐱*)−𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐤*+σn2=k(𝐱*,𝐱*)−𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐤*+σn2.

Substituting these into the Gaussian predictive distribution from Equation 11 gives:
p(f_* \mid \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(f_* \;\middle|\; \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y},\; k(\mathbf{x}_*,\mathbf{x}_*) - \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_* + \sigma_n^2\right). \qquad(17)p(f*∣𝐱*,𝐗,𝐲)=𝒩(f*|𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐲,k(𝐱*,𝐱*)−𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐤*+σn2).(17)

The important observation here is that \boldsymbol{\phi}𝛟 has vanished entirely. The predictions now depend only on kernel evaluations between data points. We are completely free to specify kk directly, and we never need to construct an explicit feature map. In particular, if we allow M \to \inftyM→∞ many basis functions, and we define kk to be the corresponding limiting inner product, the model becomes non-parametric. The functions complexity grows with the data rather than being fixed in advance (Williams 1996; D. J. MacKay 1998). Williams (1996) showed that a Bayesian neural network with an infinite number of hidden units and a Gaussian weight prior converges to a GP, formally showing the connection between the weight-space and function-space views.

This is the so called function-space perspective. Instead of reasoning about a weight vector \mathbf{w}𝐰, we place a prior directly over functions, characterised entirely by kk. The result is a Gaussian process.

sec.title: 3. Gaussian Processes
sec.p: Formally, a Gaussian process is a collection of random variables, any finite number of which have a joint Gaussian distribution (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). A GP is fully specified by its mean function m(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x})]m(𝐱)=𝔼[f(𝐱)] and covariance function (or kernel) k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \mathbb{E}[(f(\mathbf{x}) - m(\mathbf{x}))(f(\mathbf{x}') - m(\mathbf{x}'))] = \operatorname{Cov}[f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}')] k(𝐱,𝐱′)=𝔼[(f(𝐱)−m(𝐱))(f(𝐱′)−m(𝐱′))]=Cov[f(𝐱),f(𝐱′)]

We write f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m, k)f∼𝒢𝒫(m,k) to denote that ff is a random function drawn from a GP with mean mm and kernel kk. The GP provides a prior directly over functions directly, rather than over a finite parameter vector as in the weight-space view of Section 2.4.

sec.title: 3.1 The GP Prior
sec.p:
Placing a GP prior on ff gives a “prior over functions”. Evaluating ff at any finite collection of inputs \mathbf{X} = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n\}𝐗={𝐱1,…,𝐱n} gives a joint Gaussian over the corresponding function values \mathbf{f} = [f(\mathbf{x}_1), \ldots, f(\mathbf{x}_n)]^\top𝐟=[f(𝐱1),…,f(𝐱n)]⊤,
\mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, K), \qquad(18)𝐟∣𝐗∼𝒩(𝐦,K),(18)

where [\mathbf{m}]_i = m(\mathbf{x}_i)[𝐦]i=m(𝐱i) and K_{ij} = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)Kij=k(𝐱i,𝐱j). This property that every finite-dimensional marginal is Gaussian is a defining characteristic of the process (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; Williams and Rasmussen 1995). In regression, it is standard to take m \equiv 0m≡0, as any non-zero prior mean can be absorbed into the model or estimated from data (D. J. MacKay 1998), and by doing so we focus attention on the kernel as the key modelling choice.

sec.title: 3.2 Kernels and Covariance Functions
sec.p: All of the structure of the prior is encoded in the kernel kk. The kernel determines how function values co-vary across input space: inputs that are close according to kk will have strongly correlated function values, while distant inputs are nearly independent. Kernel hyper-parameters directly control interpretable properties such as the characteristic length-scale (how rapidly the function varies), the output scale (the typical amplitude), and whether the function is stationary or periodic. Figure 1 illustrates this with two common choices: the squared exponential (SE) kernel, which produces infinitely differentiable functions whose roughness is controlled by a length-scale parameter \ellℓ, and the periodic kernel, whose period parameter pp fixes the repetition frequency of the sampled functions.

caption.p: Figure 1: Prior samples from GPs with the SE kernel (left) and the periodic kernel (right) under varying hyperparameters.

sec.p:
The SE kernel, also called the radial basis function (RBF) kernel, is defined as
k_{\text{SE}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|^2}{2\ell^2}\right), \qquad(19)kSE(𝐱,𝐱′)=σf2exp(−∥𝐱−𝐱′∥22ℓ2),(19)

and is the most widely used GP kernel in practice (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). A small \ellℓ allows the function to vary rapidly over short distances, producing rough wiggly samples, while a large \ellℓ enforces smoothly varying functions. The periodic kernel,
k_{\text{per}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{2\sin^2\!\left(\pi|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'|/p\right)}{\ell^2}\right), \qquad(20)kper(𝐱,𝐱′)=σf2exp(−2sin2(π|𝐱−𝐱′|/p)ℓ2),(20)

explicitly encodes a repeating structure with period pp, making it suitable for modelling seasonal or cyclical signals (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). Kernels can also be combined — sums and products of valid kernels are themselves valid kernels — enabling the construction of structured priors that capture multiple scales or mixed behaviours (Rasmussen and Williams 2008, ch.~4; Schölkopf 2002).

sec.title: 3.3 Choosing Kernel Hyperparameters
sec.p: The kernel hyperparameters \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉 (e.g. length-scale \ellℓ, output scale \sigma_f^2σf2, noise variance \sigma_n^2σn2) are not specified by the GP directly, and must be estimated from data. The standard approach is to maximise the log marginal likelihood (LML) of the observed data under the GP model, also known as type-II maximum likelihood or empirical Bayes (D. J. C. MacKay 1992; D. J. MacKay 1998; Rasmussen and Williams 2008),

This LML has 3 interpretable terms: the first encourages the model to fit the data well, the second penalises overly complex models that can fit many functions, and the third is a constant that ensures the likelihood is properly normalised. The LML is typically maximised using gradient-based optimisation (e.g. L-BFGS or Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015)), which is tractable for exact GPs since the LML and its gradients can be computed in \mathcal{O}(n^3)𝒪(n3) time via Cholesky decomposition of K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}K+σn2𝐈 (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). However, the LML is non-convex and can have multiple local optima, so it is common to perform multiple random restarts to increase the chances of finding a good solution. Additionally, since kernel hyperparameters are typically constrained to be positive, it is standard practice to optimise them in log-space to ensure positivity and improve numerical stability.

sec.title: 3.5 Training a GP
sec.p: We showed in Section 3.3 that the kernel hyper-parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉 can be estimated by maximising the log marginal likelihood (LML) of the observed data. The LML is a non-convex function of \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉, but its gradients can be computed efficiently using matrix calculus and automatic differentiation, enabling gradient-based optimisation methods such as L-BFGS or Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) to find good hyperparameter settings. However, computing the LML and its gradients requires an \mathcal{O}(n^3)𝒪(n3) Cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}K+σn2𝐈, which is tractable for moderate nn but becomes prohibitive for large datasets, motivating the development of sparse and approximate inference methods for scaling GPs to larger problems (Snelson and Ghahramani 2006; Titsias 2009).

sec.title: 3.5.1 Gradient of the Log Marginal Likelihood
sec.p: We have the LML expression from Equation 21: \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y} - \frac{1}{2}\log |K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}| - \frac{n}{2}\log 2\pi.logp(𝐲∣𝐗,𝛉)=−12𝐲⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐲−12log|K+σn2𝐈|−n2log2π.

The gradient of the LML with respect to a hyperparameter \theta_jθj can be derived using the matrix derivative trace formula (Rasmussen and Williams 2008, Equation 5.9), yielding: \frac{\partial \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} \frac{\partial (K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})}{\partial \theta_j} (K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{y} - \frac{1}{2}\text{tr}\!\left((K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} \frac{\partial (K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})}{\partial \theta_j}\right). ∂logp(𝐲∣𝐗,𝛉)∂θj=12𝐲⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1∂(K+σn2𝐈)∂θj(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐲−12tr((K+σn2𝐈)−1∂(K+σn2𝐈)∂θj).

This expression consists of two terms: the first encourages the model to fit the data well by increasing the LML when the hyperparameter leads to a better fit, while the second penalises overly complex models by decreasing the LML when the hyperparameter increases model complexity. These gradients can be computed efficiently using automatic differentiation libraries, allowing for effective optimisation of the hyperparameters.

In practice, the training loop iterates: (1) evaluate the negative LML via Cholesky factorisation of K_\theta + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}Kθ+σn2𝐈; (2) backpropagate to obtain \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta_j∂ℒ/∂θj for each hyperparameter; (3) apply an update step (e.g. Adam). Because the LML is non-convex, running multiple random restarts and keeping the solution with the lowest negative LML is common practice. Positive-constrained hyperparameters (\ellℓ, \sigma_f^2σf2, \sigma_n^2σn2) are parameterised in log-space throughout to ensure positivity and improve the conditioning of the optimisation landscape. Figure 3 illustrates the effect of training: a GP with a poorly initialised length-scale produces an oversmoothed, miscalibrated fit, while the same model after 50 Adam steps accurately recovers the latent function.

sec.title: 3.6 Prediction
sec.p: With hyperparameters fixed at their optimised values \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}𝛉̂, prediction reduces to evaluating the posterior from Equation 24 at any desired test location \mathbf{x}_*𝐱*. The dominant cost is forming the Cholesky factorisation LL^\top = K_{\hat{\theta}} + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I}LL⊤=Kθ̂+σn2𝐈, which is \mathcal{O}(n^3)𝒪(n3) and performed once. Once cached, evaluating the predictive mean and variance at a new point requires only two triangular solves and a kernel evaluation, costing \mathcal{O}(n)𝒪(n) per point — making prediction cheap at test time once training has been completed.

The predictive variance at a test point \mathbf{x}_*𝐱* decomposes naturally into two contributions:
\mathbb{V}[f_* \mid \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}, \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}] = \underbrace{k(\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{x}_*) - \mathbf{k}_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_*}_{\text{epistemic (reducible)}} + \underbrace{\sigma_n^2}_{\text{aleatoric (irreducible)}}, \qquad(25)𝕍[f*∣𝐱*,𝐗,𝐲,𝛉̂]=k(𝐱*,𝐱*)−𝐤*⊤(K+σn2𝐈)−1𝐤*⏟epistemic (reducible)+σn2⏟aleatoric (irreducible),(25)

where the first term is the epistemic uncertainty — reflecting ignorance about the latent function ff — and the second is the aleatoric noise variance (Kendall and Gal 2017). The epistemic component shrinks as training observations accumulate near \mathbf{x}_*𝐱*, and recovers the full prior variance k(\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{x}_*)k(𝐱*,𝐱*) only in regions with no data. The aleatoric term \sigma_n^2σn2 is present whenever a noisy observation y_* = f(\mathbf{x}_*) + \epsilon_*y*=f(𝐱*)+ϵ* is requested, but absent from the latent predictive distribution over f(\mathbf{x}_*)f(𝐱*) itself. This separation is a distinctive strength of the GP framework: the two sources of uncertainty are quantified separately and automatically, without requiring any post-hoc calibration (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; Kendall and Gal 2017).

This is visible in Figure 2: uncertainty collapses near the training observations (low epistemic uncertainty) and inflates in the gaps and at the extrapolation boundaries (high epistemic uncertainty), while the posterior mean threads through the data.

sec.title: 4. Deep Gaussian Processes
sec.p: The previous section established that GPs provide closed-form predictions and uncertainty estimates, governed entirely by the choice of kernel. However, the expressiveness of a single-layer GP is fundamentally constrained by this kernel: a stationary kernel like the squared exponential encodes a fixed notion of smoothness across the entire input space, which may not match real-world data where patterns vary in complexity across different regions.

Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) address this by composing multiple GP layers hierarchically. Rather than relying on hand-crafted kernels, DGPs learn representations at multiple levels of abstraction, much like deep neural networks, while retaining Bayesian uncertainty quantification. This section formalises the DGP model and shows why exact inference becomes intractable in the deep setting, motivating the approximate methods of Section 5.

sec.title: 4.1 Definition and Model Formulation
sec.p: DGPs extend standard GPs by composing multiple GP layers in a hierarchical structure (Damianou and Lawrence 2013). Instead of a single mapping from inputs to outputs, DGPs construct a chain of latent function spaces, each transforming the previous layer.
An LL-layer DGP is defined by a sequence of latent functions \{f^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}{f(ℓ)}ℓ=1L where each function is drawn from a GP prior conditioned on the output of the previous:

with the convention \mathbf{F}^{(0)} = \mathbf{X}𝐅(0)=𝐗 (the observed inputs). Each layer applies a freshly drawn GP function to the outputs of the previous layer — the first layer warps the raw inputs, the second warps those warped values, and so on. The model is a learned chain of transformations, each inheriting all the uncertainty of the layers before it.
For observed inputs \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_0}𝐗∈ℝn×d0 and outputs \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n𝐲∈ℝn, the generative model proceeds as:

When \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ−1) is held fixed, this is identical to a standard GP prior — layer \ellℓ behaves exactly like a regular GP evaluated at those inputs. The difficulty arises only when \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ−1) is random: the covariance matrix K^{(\ell)}K(ℓ) then becomes a random variable itself, and integrating over it no longer yields a closed form.
The directed graph structure implies that each layer depends only on its immediate predecessor (a Markov property), leading to a factorised joint prior:

In plain terms: once you know what layer \ell\!-\!1ℓ−1 output, knowledge of all earlier layers gives no additional information about layer \ellℓ. sec.p: The expressiveness of DGPs over standard GPs comes from this composition (Damianou and Lawrence 2013; Dunlop et al. 2018). Even when each layer uses a stationary kernel, the composed function yields a non-stationary process. Consider the covariance of g = f^{(2)} \circ f^{(1)}g=f(2)∘f(1):

The composed covariance is therefore not simply a function of \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'𝐱−𝐱′, making the process non-stationary. This input-dependent structure lets DGPs model functions with varying smoothness and lengthscale across input space. To see why this is useful, imagine fitting a signal that is smooth in some regions and rapidly varying in others: a single GP with a fixed lengthscale must compromise, while a DGP can learn to “stretch” the input space in smooth regions and “compress” it in complex regions through f^{(1)}f(1), giving the second layer an effectively adapted coordinate system. sec.title: 4.2 Intractability of Exact Inference
sec.p: For standard single-layer GPs, the posterior p(f_* \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y})p(f*∣𝐗,𝐲) and marginal likelihood p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X})p(𝐲∣𝐗) give closed-form expressions due to Gaussian conjugacy (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). In DGPs this is lost because composition of GPs produces a non-Gaussian joint distribution.
The marginal likelihood requires integrating out all latent functions:

where \mathbf{F}^{(0)} = \mathbf{X}𝐅(0)=𝐗. This integral has no closed-form solution for L \geq 2L≥2 with non-degenerate kernels. The fundamental obstacle is that the covariance matrix K^{(\ell)}K(ℓ) at each layer is a nonlinear function of \mathbf{F}^{(\ell-1)}𝐅(ℓ−1) — the very variables being integrated over — so the integral cannot be reorganised into the product-of-Gaussians form that makes single-layer GP inference tractable.

To see why, consider a two-layer DGP. The covariance matrix K^{(2)}K(2) depends on \mathbf{F}^{(1)}𝐅(1) through [K^{(2)}]_{ij} = k^{(2)}(f_i^{(1)}, f_j^{(1)})[K(2)]ij=k(2)(fi(1),fj(1)). For the squared exponential kernel:
this is a nonlinear function of the Gaussian random variables (f_i^{(1)}, f_j^{(1)})(fi(1),fj(1)). The integral

is a mixture of Gaussians with continuously varying covariance. Intuitively, for every possible realisation of \mathbf{F}^{(1)}𝐅(1) there is a different Gaussian over \mathbf{F}^{(2)}𝐅(2); marginalising out \mathbf{F}^{(1)}𝐅(1) means averaging together infinitely many Gaussians with different shapes, producing a result that is heavier-tailed and more complex than any individual Gaussian component. No closed form exists for these integrals.

As well as the intractability of the marginal likelihood, the resulting distribution over outputs is non-Gaussian. Consider a two-layer DGP with first-layer outputs h_1 = f^{(1)}(x_1)h1=f(1)(x1), h_2 = f^{(1)}(x_2)h2=f(1)(x2). From the GP prior:

alternatives.tex-math: \begin{bmatrix} h_1 \\ h_2 \end{bmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{bmatrix} k^{(1)}_{11} & k^{(1)}_{12} \\ k^{(1)}_{12} & k^{(1)}_{22} \end{bmatrix}\right). \qquad(36)

sec.p: Conditioned on (h_1, h_2)(h1,h2), the outputs follow:

alternatives.tex-math: \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} \Bigg| h_1, h_2 \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{bmatrix} k^{(2)}(h_1, h_1) & k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2) \\ k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2) & k^{(2)}(h_2, h_2) \end{bmatrix}\right). \qquad(37)

sec.p: The marginal distribution
is a continuous mixture of Gaussians with varying covariance matrices. Since k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2)k(2)(h1,h2) is a nonlinear function of (h_1, h_2)(h1,h2), this mixture is not Gaussian.

This can be verified by noting that a Gaussian mixture with continuously varying covariance matrices produces a distribution whose higher moments (e.g., kurtosis) differ from those of any single Gaussian. In particular, the marginal density of y_1y1 under such a mixture is generally heavier-tailed than any individual Gaussian component (Gelman et al. 2025).
The posterior over all latent functions is:
Since both the numerator (a product of coupled Gaussians) and the denominator (the intractable marginal likelihood) lack closed forms, exact posterior computation is infeasible.

Even numerical integration is impractical. The integration is over \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} n d_\ell∑ℓ=1Lndℓ continuous variables, which cannot be factored across layers due to kernel dependencies. This motivates the development of approximate inference methods for DGP learning (Damianou and Lawrence 2013; Salimbeni and Deisenroth 2017).

sec.title: 5. Learning in GP and DGP Models
sec.p: The previous section showed that DGPs offer richer modelling capacity than standard GPs, but at the cost of tractable inference. This section develops the framework for learning in both settings.

We briefly revisit hyperparameter learning in standard GPs — focusing on how the marginal likelihood arises by integrating out function values — to identify the structural property that is lost in DGPs. We then introduce variational inference for approximating intractable posteriors, build to sparse variational methods that reduce computation from O(n^3)O(n3) to O(nm^2)O(nm2), and finally extend these ideas to DGPs through doubly stochastic variational inference.

sec.title: 5.1 Learning in Standard GPs
sec.p: As established in Section 3.3, GP hyperparameters \boldsymbol{\theta}𝛉 are learned by maximising the log marginal likelihood (LML). It is worth seeing explicitly how this LML arises by integrating out the latent function values \mathbf{f}𝐟, since this tractability is precisely what is lost in DGPs.

Starting from the GP prior \mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})𝐟∣𝐗∼𝒩(𝟎,K𝛉) and likelihood \mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{f} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{f}, \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I})𝐲∣𝐟∼𝒩(𝐟,σn2𝐈), Gaussian–Gaussian conjugacy (Bernardo and Smith 2000) allows the integral over function values to be computed in closed form:
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \int p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{f}) p(\mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \, d\mathbf{f} = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{0}, K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}), \qquad(40)p(𝐲∣𝐗,𝛉)=∫p(𝐲∣𝐟)p(𝐟∣𝐗,𝛉)d𝐟=𝒩(𝐲∣𝟎,K𝛉+σn2𝐈),(40) giving the LML of Equation 21. The key step is that a Gaussian prior on \mathbf{f}𝐟 multiplied by a Gaussian likelihood in \mathbf{y}𝐲 integrates analytically: the product of two Gaussians is proportional to a Gaussian, so the \mathbf{f}𝐟-integral collapses to a single multivariate normal with covariance K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}K𝛉+σn2𝐈. This closed-form collapse is precisely what is lost in DGPs, where the covariance depends on random latent variables. Hyperparameters are found via gradient ascent; the gradient with respect to \theta_jθj is (Rasmussen and Williams 2008):

where \boldsymbol{\alpha} = K_y^{-1} \mathbf{y}𝛂=Ky−1𝐲 and K_y = K_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}Ky=K𝛉+σn2𝐈. The matrix \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\alpha}^\top - K_y^{-1}𝛂𝛂⊤−Ky−1 has a natural interpretation: \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\alpha}^\top𝛂𝛂⊤ is a rank-one outer product that captures how the data predicts itself under the current model, while K_y^{-1}Ky−1 reflects the full model uncertainty; a large positive difference for \partial K_y / \partial \theta_j∂Ky/∂θj indicates that increasing \theta_jθj improves the data fit more than it increases model complexity. This follows from the matrix calculus identities \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \log|K| = \operatorname{tr}(K^{-1} \frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta})∂∂θlog|K|=tr(K−1∂K∂θ) and \frac{\partial K^{-1}}{\partial \theta} = -K^{-1} \frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta} K^{-1}∂K−1∂θ=−K−1∂K∂θK−1.

Each gradient step requires K_y^{-1}Ky−1, computed via Cholesky decomposition at O(n^3)O(n3) cost with O(n^2)O(n2) storage (Rasmussen and Williams 2008). For small to moderate datasets (n \lesssim 10{,}000n≲10,000) this is typically feasible and remains the gold standard: the LML gradients are exact, and no approximation is introduced beyond the choice of kernel. For larger datasets the cubic cost becomes prohibitive, motivating the sparse variational approach of the following section.

sec.title: 5.2 Variational Inference
sec.p: When exact inference is intractable, variational inference provides a principled approximation framework (Jordan et al. 1999; Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe 2017). The idea is to approximate the true posterior p(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{y})p(𝐳∣𝐲) with a tractable distribution q(\mathbf{z})q(𝐳), chosen to minimise the Kullback–Leibler divergence between them.
For latent variables \mathbf{z}𝐳 and observations \mathbf{y}𝐲, the log marginal likelihood separates as:
where the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is:

Since KL divergence is non-negative, \mathcal{L}(q) \leq \log p(\mathbf{y})ℒ(q)≤logp(𝐲) with equality when q(\mathbf{z}) = p(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{y})q(𝐳)=p(𝐳∣𝐲). This is the central insight: rather than computing the intractable posterior directly, we turn the problem into an optimisation — find the qq that maximises the ELBO, which simultaneously tightens the bound and minimises the error of our approximation.
To show Equation 42, start from the definition of KL divergence:

Rearranging gives Equation 42. Since \operatorname{KL}(q \| p)KL(q∥p) cannot be computed directly (it is intractable), we instead maximise the ELBO, which is equivalent to minimising KL divergence. This replaces an intractable posterior computation with a tractable optimisation problem — the core trade of variational inference.

The second form Equation 43 illuminates the ELBO’s structure. The expected log-likelihood \mathbb{E}_{q}[\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{z})]𝔼q[logp(𝐲∣𝐳)] encourages qq to concentrate where the data is well-explained, while the KL term \operatorname{KL}(q \| p(\mathbf{z}))KL(q∥p(𝐳)) regularises qq toward the prior, preventing overfitting (Bishop 2006). This trade-off mirrors the data-fit versus complexity balance in exact Bayesian inference.

For the models in this dissertation, variational inference serves two purposes: enabling scalability to large datasets, and handling the hierarchical structure of DGPs where function values at each layer cannot be analytically integrated out. The latent variables \mathbf{z}𝐳 correspond to function values \mathbf{f}𝐟, and the variational distribution is usually chosen to be Gaussian:

with variational parameters \mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^n𝐦∈ℝn and S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}S∈ℝn×n (positive definite). This balances expressiveness with computational tractability. The expectations under qq can often be computed analytically for standard likelihood functions.
With this Gaussian choice, the KL term has closed form:

where KK is the prior covariance. Each term has a clear role: \mathbf{m}^\top K^{-1} \mathbf{m}𝐦⊤K−1𝐦 penalises the variational mean for straying far from zero in units of the prior length-scale; \operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}S)tr(K−1S) penalises the variational covariance for being larger than the prior; and \log|K| - \log|S|log|K|−log|S| is a log-volume ratio that rewards qq for being more concentrated than the prior. Together they ensure qq cannot deviate from p(\mathbf{f})p(𝐟) without paying a KL cost. Optimisation over a full-rank matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}S∈ℝn×n still involves O(n^2)O(n2) parameters, which becomes problematic for large nn. The key to resolving this is to restrict the variational family to a lower-dimensional subspace defined by m \ll nm≪n inducing points, as developed in the following section.

sec.title: 5.3 Sparse Variational GPs
sec.p: The O(n^3)O(n3) cost of standard GP inference becomes prohibitive for large datasets. Sparse methods address this by using m \ll nm≪n inducing points that summarise the data, reducing complexity to O(nm^2)O(nm2) (Quinonero-Candela and Rasmussen 2005; Titsias 2009).

Consider inducing inputs \mathbf{Z} = \{\mathbf{z}_j\}_{j=1}^m𝐙={𝐳j}j=1m with function values \mathbf{u} = f(\mathbf{Z}) \in \mathbb{R}^m𝐮=f(𝐙)∈ℝm. From the prior, the joint distribution of function values \mathbf{f}𝐟 at training inputs and inducing values \mathbf{u}𝐮 is:

The cross-covariance K_{fu}Kfu encodes how strongly each training point correlates with each inducing point: if inducing points are placed where the data concentrates, K_{fu}Kfu will be large and the mm inducing values will carry most of the information about the nn function values.

In practice the two sources of noise act independently: increasing the minibatch size |\mathcal{B}||ℬ| reduces noise from data sampling, while increasing the sample count SS reduces noise from layer propagation.

In effect, the randomness is “pushed outside” the computation graph, so automatic differentiation can treat \muμ and \sigmaσ as ordinary differentiable variables.

sec.title: 6. Deep Gaussian Processes for Financial Risk Modeling
sec.p: Gaussian processes are well-established Bayesian non-parametric models for regression and classification, and GP-based recurrent extensions have also been used for time-series modelling (Rasmussen and Williams 2008; Williams and Rasmussen 1995; Mattos et al. 2016). Deep Gaussian processes extend this framework by composing multiple GP layers, giving a more expressive probabilistic model while retaining an explicit treatment of predictive uncertainty (Damianou and Lawrence 2013; Salimbeni and Deisenroth 2017).

In finance, GP-based methods have been applied to credit-risk and credit-rating problems (Mahajan et al. 2022; Huang 2011), volatility forecasting (Munoz-Gonzalez, Lazaro-Gredilla, and Figueiras-Vidal 2014), algorithmic trading strategy identification (Yang et al. 2015), and market-risk approximation for trading portfolios (Lehdili, Oswald, and Nguyen 2025). Basel III and the wider Basel Framework make banks’ capital requirements explicitly risk-sensitive, so reliable estimates of probability of default (PD) and other loss-related quantities are important for both regulatory compliance and internal risk management (“Basel III: A Global Regulatory Framework for More Resilient Banks and Banking Systems” 2011). Against that background, comparing GPs and DGPs for credit-risk prediction is well motivated. At the same time, the finance literature cited above is still dominated by standard GP variants, with direct DGP applications appearing much less common. This section therefore compares GPs and DGPs with standard machine learning baselines on financial datasets, focusing on both predictive performance and the quality of uncertainty quantification, while also considering computational cost and interpretability.

sec.title: 6.1 Credit Card Probability of Default
sec.p: The first empirical study uses the UCI default of credit card clients dataset (Yeh and Lien 2009). The dataset contains 30,000 observations and 23 predictor variables describing credit limit, age, sex, education, marital status, six months of repayment-status history, six months of bill amounts, and six months of repayment amounts. The target is whether a client defaults on the next payment cycle. This is a useful test-bed for PD modelling because it combines moderate class imbalance with a decision problem in which both ranking quality and probability calibration matter.

The data were cleaned using the protocol implemented in the experimental pipeline. Undocumented education and marriage codes were collapsed into “other” categories, skewed monetary variables were log-transformed, categorical variables were one-hot encoded, and continuous variables were standardised before model fitting. To support both model selection and post-hoc probability calibration, the final protocol used a stratified four-way split: 15,000 observations for model fitting, 3,000 for validation, 6,000 for calibration, and 6,000 for the final test set. The validation split is used only for model-selection logic in XGBoost; the calibration split is reserved for Platt scaling and isotonic regression; the test split remains untouched until the final evaluation stage. The implementation of this split logic is reproduced in Appendix Section 6.6.1.

caption.p: Figure 5: Overview of the UCI credit card default dataset. Panel (a) shows the class balance, while panel (b) summarises recent repayment-status behaviour by outcome. The default class remains a minority class, but defaulters exhibit systematically worse repayment-status codes in the most recent months.

sec.p: The model set consists of three standard tabular baselines and three Gaussian-process models. The classical baselines are logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. The probabilistic models are a sparse variational GP (SVGP) and two deep sparse variational GPs with two and three layers respectively. The SVGP is trained with mini-batch stochastic variational inference using the variational ELBO (Hensman, Fusi, and Lawrence 2013), while the deep GP models use the doubly stochastic variational construction of Salimbeni and Deisenroth (Salimbeni and Deisenroth 2017). The concrete training loops used in the experiment are reproduced in Appendix Section 6.6.3 and Appendix Section 6.6.4. The main comparison uses each model in its native form. A second calibration study then evaluates two pre-hoc interventions for the classical baselines by removing the imbalance weighting used in the raw baseline, followed by two post-hoc calibration methods, Platt scaling (Platt 1999) and isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan 2002), fitted on the held-out calibration split.

Model quality is assessed along four dimensions. First, discriminative ability is measured using ROC-AUC and average precision. Second, thresholded classification behaviour at the conventional 0.50.5 cutoff is summarised with precision, recall, F1, balanced accuracy, and MCC. Third, probability quality is assessed with the Brier score, log loss, and expected calibration error (ECE). Fourth, computational cost is recorded as total training time. This combination is appropriate for a PD setting because a model that ranks well but produces poorly calibrated probabilities is still problematic for risk-sensitive decisions.

sec.title: 6.1.1 Discriminative Performance

caption.p: Figure 6: ROC and precision-recall curves for the six main models. XGBoost, SVGP, and the two DGP variants form the leading group on ranking metrics, with the GP-family models matching the strongest tree baseline closely.

sec.p: On ranking performance, the strongest models are XGBoost, SVGP, and the two DGP variants. XGBoost achieves the highest ROC-AUC at 0.7763, while DSVGP-2L and SVGP are effectively tied just behind it at 0.7777 and 0.7776 respectively. Average precision tells a similar story: DSVGP-2L is slightly best at 0.5523, followed closely by SVGP at 0.5503 and random forest at 0.5501. Logistic regression is clearly weaker as a ranker, which is consistent with the expectation that a linear model cannot fully capture the non-linear interactions present in repayment-history and balance behaviour.

At the default 0.50.5 threshold, the picture is different. XGBoost attains the strongest F1 score among the main raw models at 0.5395, with random forest close behind at 0.5303. The GP-family models are more conservative positive callers: their precision is materially higher, but their recall is lower. For example, DSVGP-2L reaches precision 0.6608 with recall 0.3700, whereas XGBoost reaches precision 0.4839 with recall 0.6096. This is a useful reminder that ranking metrics and threshold metrics answer different questions. In a credit-risk context, the preferred operating point should depend on the institution’s cost trade-off between missed defaults and unnecessary interventions, not on the default threshold alone.

sec.title: 6.1.2 Native Calibration

caption.p: Figure 7: Reliability diagrams for the main six-model comparison. The GP-family models are close to the diagonal in their native form, while the classical baselines are materially miscalibrated before any post-hoc correction.

sec.p: The native calibration results are the clearest strength of the GP-family models. DSVGP-2L obtains the lowest Brier score among the six raw models at 0.1351 and the lowest ECE at 0.0111. SVGP is almost identical, with Brier 0.1356 and ECE 0.0127. DSVGP-3L remains very strong, although slightly worse calibrated than the shallower DGP. By contrast, the raw classical baselines are substantially miscalibrated. Logistic regression is the weakest on this criterion, with ECE 0.2232 and Brier 0.1985. XGBoost also shows strong miscalibration in its native form, with ECE 0.2096 and Brier 0.1818. Random forest is better than the other classical models natively, but still well behind the GP-family models on probability quality.

These results matter because the dissertation is not only interested in whether a model can rank risky clients, but also whether the output probabilities can be interpreted as credible PD estimates. On that criterion, the raw GP and DGP models clearly dominate the native classical baselines.

sec.title: 6.1.3 Pre-Hoc And Post-Hoc Calibration Of Classical Baselines
sec.p: The next question is whether the calibration gap remains once the classical baselines are given explicit calibration treatment. Two types of intervention were tested. The pre-hoc intervention removes class-imbalance weighting from the classical training objective. The post-hoc intervention fits either Platt scaling or isotonic regression on the held-out calibration split, then evaluates the recalibrated probabilities on the untouched test split.

It is useful to define the three stages explicitly. The raw model means the original fitted classifier together with its native probability outputs. The pre_hoc variant changes the training objective before fitting by removing class weighting, so it can alter both the score ranking and the final probability scale. The post_hoc variant leaves the underlying fitted model unchanged and instead learns a separate mapping from held-out raw scores to calibrated probabilities. In the implementation, this happens only after the raw model has produced calibration-set probabilities, as shown in Appendix Section 6.6.2. Strictly speaking, pre-hoc calibration is not a separate calibration layer at all; it is a training-time intervention that may improve calibration indirectly by changing the learned classifier.

caption.p: Figure 8: Calibration comparison for the classical baselines. Each panel compares the raw model, the pre-hoc unweighted variant, and the two post-hoc calibrated variants for one baseline family. Post-hoc calibration removes most of the miscalibration visible in the raw models.
Calibration study for the classical baselines. The raw models are compared with a pre-hoc unweighted variant and two post-hoc calibration methods fitted on the dedicated calibration split.

sec.p: The pre-hoc results show that training-time changes alone help only partially. Removing the imbalance weighting improves the calibration of logistic regression and random forest substantially, but it often shifts the decision boundary toward very conservative behaviour. XGBoost without class weighting is particularly poor at the default threshold, with recall collapsing even though its ranking metrics remain competitive. In other words, pre-hoc changes can improve probability quality, but they also alter classification behaviour in ways that are not obviously desirable for PD screening.

The post-hoc results are more important. After calibration, the classical baselines close most of the calibration gap. Random forest plus Platt scaling reduces ECE from 0.0862 to 0.0136, while also improving the Brier score from 0.1458 to 0.1362. XGBoost plus Platt scaling reduces ECE from 0.2096 to 0.0109 and Brier score from 0.1818 to 0.1365. Isotonic regression yields similarly strong improvements, especially for logistic regression and XGBoost. This means that the main empirical story is more nuanced than the raw comparison alone suggests: GP and DGP models are clearly best in native calibration, but strong classical baselines can be made almost equally well calibrated once an explicit post-hoc calibration layer is introduced.

Because post-hoc calibration changes the probability scale, threshold-dependent metrics must be recomputed after recalibration rather than inherited from the raw model. The experiment therefore recalculates full threshold sweeps for the raw and post-hoc variants and exports a supplementary threshold-optima table. Table Table 1 reports the F1-optimal operating point for each classical baseline and its recalibrated variants; the exported artifact also records the thresholds that maximize precision, recall, balanced accuracy, MCC, and specificity.

caption.p: Table 1: F1-optimal operating thresholds for the classical baselines before and after post-hoc recalibration. The full supplementary threshold summary also records the thresholds that maximize precision, recall, balanced accuracy, MCC, and specificity.

Figure 9: F1 and recall as functions of the decision threshold for the raw and Platt-calibrated classical baselines. Recalibration improves probability quality, but it also shifts the threshold at which the best operating trade-off is obtained.

sec.p: The threshold-optima summary shows that recalibration materially shifts the best operating threshold even when it leaves ranking performance almost unchanged. Logistic regression reaches its best F1 at a threshold of 0.60 in raw form, but at 0.30 after Platt scaling. Random forest moves from 0.45 to 0.30, and XGBoost from 0.50 to 0.25. The corresponding best-F1 values improve only slightly. This is exactly the pattern one would expect from a calibration layer: it mostly repairs the probability scale rather than the underlying ordering of cases. For Platt scaling, ROC-AUC and average precision are therefore almost unchanged because the mapping is monotone; isotonic regression can perturb ranking slightly by introducing flat regions and score ties, but its main effect is still on probability quality rather than separability.

That finding is valuable rather than inconvenient. It sharpens the comparison. The GP-family models do not require an extra calibration stage to reach strong probability quality, whereas the classical baselines do. Once that extra stage is allowed, however, random forest and XGBoost become much more credible PD models than their raw probabilities suggest.

There are also important limitations. Post-hoc calibration consumes a dedicated calibration split, so it reduces the data available for model fitting unless an external validation sample is available. It cannot repair a fundamentally weak ranker; it only remaps the scores the model already produces. It also means that threshold selection must be revisited after recalibration, because the threshold that maximizes F1, recall, or balanced accuracy can shift sharply even when ROC-AUC barely moves. Isotonic regression adds a further risk of overfitting when the calibration sample is small or unrepresentative. For these reasons, post-hoc calibration should be treated as an additional modeling stage rather than a free afterthought.

sec.title: 6.1.4 Threshold Behaviour And Computational Cost

caption.p: Figure 10: Threshold sensitivity of the six main raw models. The optimal threshold differs materially across models, which reinforces that a fixed 0.50.5 rule is only a diagnostic baseline rather than a business-optimal operating point.

Figure 11: Training-time versus calibration trade-off for the six main raw models. The GP-family models achieve the best native calibration, but at a much higher computational cost than the classical baselines.

sec.p: The threshold sweep confirms that the default 0.50.5 cutoff is not an especially meaningful operating point for cross-model comparison. The GP-family models achieve their strongest behaviour at thresholds lower than the tree baselines, which is consistent with their more conservative raw score distributions. After post-hoc calibration, the classical baselines also move toward lower best thresholds, reinforcing that a fixed operating cutoff should not be carried over mechanically from the raw model to the recalibrated one. This is another reason to separate ranking quality, calibration quality, and threshold behaviour rather than conflating them into a single headline metric.

Computationally, the contrast is stark. Logistic regression trains in 0.022 seconds, XGBoost in 0.318 seconds, and random forest in 3.274 seconds. SVGP requires 117.7 seconds, DSVGP-2L requires 137.4 seconds, and DSVGP-3L requires 543.2 seconds. The deeper GP architecture therefore offers no decisive performance gain over the two-layer DGP while costing roughly four times as much to train. For this dataset, DSVGP-2L is the more defensible deep GP variant.

sec.title: 6.1.5 Additional Diagnostics

caption.p: Figure 12: Feature-importance summaries for the classical baselines. Repayment history and recent bill/payment behaviour dominate the most predictive variables, which is consistent with the domain interpretation of short-horizon default risk.

Figure 13: Confusion matrices for the six main raw models at a decision threshold of 0.50.5. The GP-family models make fewer positive calls than the strongest tree baselines, which explains their higher precision and lower recall.

sec.p: The classical feature-importance diagnostics are broadly consistent across model families. Recent repayment-status variables, recent bill amounts, and recent payment amounts dominate the top ranks, which is intuitively plausible for short-horizon default prediction. The confusion matrices reinforce the threshold story from above: the GP-family models generate fewer positive predictions and therefore attain higher precision at the expense of recall.

sec.title: 6.1.6 Discussion
sec.p: This experiment supports three main conclusions. First, GPs and DGPs are genuinely strong PD models on this dataset. They match the best tabular baselines on ranking metrics and are substantially better calibrated in their native form. Second, the calibration advantage is not absolute once the classical models are given proper post-hoc treatment. Random forest and XGBoost become very well calibrated after Platt scaling or isotonic regression, and in some cases their ECE is marginally better than the GP-family models. Third, computational cost matters. If a modeler wants strong native uncertainty quantification without an extra calibration stage, SVGP and especially DSVGP-2L are persuasive. If an additional calibration stage is acceptable, calibrated random forest or calibrated XGBoost offer a much cheaper route to similarly usable PD probabilities.

For the dissertation, the most defensible summary is therefore not that GP or DGP models simply dominate all alternatives. A more accurate conclusion is that GP-family models provide the strongest native probabilistic behaviour, while calibrated tree ensembles provide the strongest pragmatic challenge once post-hoc calibration is allowed. That makes this dataset a useful opening study for the broader credit-risk modelling section: it shows both why probabilistic models matter and why calibration methodology must be treated explicitly rather than assumed.
